Bioinformatics Resource Center - Rockefeller University" author: - "[http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/scATAC/](http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/scATAC/)" - "[brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu)" --- ::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"} # Single-Cell ATAC-seq with Signac (Session 4) ::: ## Overview - [Differential Accessibility Analysis](#da-analysis) - [FindMarkers for scATAC-seq](#findmarkers) - [Pseudobulk Approaches](#pseudobulk) - [Coverage Plots](#coverage-plots) - [Where to Go Next](#next-steps) # Differential Accessibility Analysis {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## What is Differential Accessibility? Having annotated our clusters, a common next question is: > **Which genomic regions are more accessible in cell type A than cell type B?** Differentially accessible (DA) peaks can point to: - **Cell-type-specific regulatory elements** — enhancers and promoters active only in certain populations - **Disease-associated regulatory variation** — e.g., patient vs. control chromatin remodelling - **State transitions** — peaks gained or lost as cells differentiate ## Considerations for DA Testing in scATAC-seq DA testing in scATAC-seq is harder than in scRNA-seq | Challenge | Why it matters | |---|---| | Binary data | Peaks are 0 or 1; count models from RNA-seq do not match this data | | High sparsity | Many zeros inflate false positives if not accounted for | | Depth confounding | Cells with more fragments appear to have more accessible peaks | | Pseudoreplication | Cells from the same individual are not independent observations | The solution depends on your experimental design — cluster markers within a single sample vs. condition comparisons across multiple donors. # FindMarkers for scATAC-seq {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## Logistic Regression with Depth as a Covariate Signac recommends **logistic regression** for single-cell DA testing. Accessibility is modelled as a binary outcome, with cell type as the predictor and **sequencing depth as a latent variable** to control for depth confounding. ## Lets grab the data We will make sure we hAve Signac loaded in and the current pbmc object. We can set our Idents(). The Idents corresponds to which are the active group being used in our dataset. Often this is cell type labels or clusters. We will set this to "predicted.id". ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(Signac) library(Seurat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Loading required package: SeuratObject ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Loading required package: sp ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` 'SeuratObject' was built under R 4.6.0 but the current version is 4.6.1; it is recomended that you reinstall 'SeuratObject' as the ABI for R may have changed ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` 'SeuratObject' was built with package 'Matrix' 1.7.5 but the current version is 1.7.6; it is recomended that you reinstall 'SeuratObject' as the ABI for 'Matrix' may have changed ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Attaching package: 'SeuratObject' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following objects are masked from 'package:base': intersect, t ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` v5.6 adds significant improvements in speed and efficiency, particularly for large datasets. For more information, see https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/announcements. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pbmc <- readRDS("data/pbmc_annotated.rds") DefaultAssay(pbmc) <- "peaks" Idents(pbmc) <- "predicted.id" ``` ::: ## Running FindMarkers We can then look for markers of a specific cell type. The provided group has to be from whichever Idents has been set i.e. if that has been set seurat_clusters, the dent provided would be a cluster number. When you supply 1 ident, it runs a comparison against all other cells. You can do a pairwise comparison by providing ident.1 and ident.2. As mentioned we will do logistic regression and add the number of counts per cell as a covariate. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} da_peaks <- FindMarkers( object = pbmc, ident.1 = "CD14+ Monocytes", only.pos = TRUE, # look for positive markers test.use = "LR", # logistic regression latent.vars = "nCount_peaks" # control for depth ) head(da_peaks) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` p_val avg_log2FC pct.1 pct.2 p_val_adj chr6-44058475-44059214 4.212500e-35 4.312910 0.626 0.042 2.596501e-30 chr20-50274658-50275567 4.124875e-34 4.352985 0.626 0.049 2.542490e-29 chr15-92803653-92804551 1.131537e-33 4.751847 0.538 0.028 6.974565e-29 chr12-109827894-109828790 4.226383e-33 4.868226 0.544 0.028 2.605058e-28 chr2-112839190-112840108 8.650538e-32 4.119971 0.538 0.045 5.332019e-27 chr22-30270592-30271507 5.489702e-30 4.570531 0.427 0.024 3.383743e-25 ``` ::: ::: ## Annotating DA Peaks to Nearest Genes There are several ways to start functional annotating peaks to genes. The easiest (and often the most parsimonious) is to use the nearest gene. We can do this easily from our DA output. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} significant_peaks <- subset(da_peaks, p_val_adj < 0.05 & avg_log2FC > 0.5) closest <- ClosestFeature(pbmc, regions = rownames(significant_peaks)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: `ClosestFeature()` was deprecated in Signac 1.17.0. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(closest[, c("gene_name", "distance", "query_region")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` gene_name distance query_region ENST00000336600 C6orf223 50862 chr6-44058475-44059214 ENST00000303004 CEBPB 81989 chr20-50274658-50275567 ENST00000557398 FAM174B 0 chr15-92803653-92804551 ENST00000538125 TRPV4 0 chr12-109827894-109828790 ENSE00001682324 IL1B 2373 chr2-112839190-112840108 ENSE00001048398 OSM 3740 chr22-30270592-30271507 ``` ::: ::: ## Peak proximity `ClosestFeature()` uses the gene annotation stored in the ChromatinAssay. Peaks more than 100 kb from any gene body are likely distal enhancers — biologically interesting but harder to interpret without co-accessibility or footprinting data. ## So are we happy with this data? The top accessible peaks are generally related to genes that are known to be associated with CD14+ Monocytes or more generally immune cell developmental genes. That said there is a peak/gene that sticks out: FAM174B. The peak is right at the gene so it's likely to be a direct effect. A quick lit review suggests that its associated with golgi and stress. It could be realtively high because Monocytes do a lot of secretion. These cells are supposed to be from a healthy patient but maybe there is some immune activation. Often there are a few peaks here and there that could make sense. It is important to rationalize these markers and assess in the context of the all the QC and other markers. * Do we have a lot of markers that do not make sense? * Does it overlap with poor quality cells or doublets? # Visualizing regions of interest {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} Another good check is to visualize the coverage at peaks and genes of interest. Our FAM174B peak overlaps the gene, but visualizing it as a track may be more revealing. Signac's `CoveragePlot()` generates this directly from the **fragment file** — no BAM file required. Each track is generated by counting fragments that overlap a position in each cell, normalised by the number of cells in that group. This is equivalent to a pseudo-bulk ATAC-seq track per cell type. ## CoveragePlot at a Gene The most unique peak region seems to be a little more downstream, so maybe it is actually a specific enhancer. This could be an intronic enhancer?? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} DefaultAssay(pbmc) <- "peaks" CoveragePlot(object = pbmc, region = "FAM174B", expression.assay = "RNA", extend.upstream = 500, extend.downstream = 10000) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0. ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead. ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the Signac package. Please report the issue at . ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: `aes_string()` was deprecated in ggplot2 3.0.0. ℹ Please use tidy evaluation idioms with `aes()`. ℹ See also `vignette("ggplot2-in-packages")` for more information. ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the Signac package. Please report the issue at . ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Session4_files/figure-html/coveragePlot-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The plot shows, from top to bottom: per-cell-type fragment coverage tracks, the called peaks, and the gene model. ## Lets plot the peak directly Instead of specifying the gene as a region, we can specify a peak. We will subset our da_peaks to the TRPV4 peak and give that to CoveragePlot. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top_peak <- closest$query_region[closest$gene_name == "TRPV4"][1] CoveragePlot(object = pbmc, region = top_peak, extend.upstream = 1000, extend.downstream = 1000) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: Removed 106 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_segment()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_segment()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Session4_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Lets check known quantity For comparison lets check a known quantitiy: IL1B is a known to be highest in CD14+ Monocytes, but also CD16+ Monocytes and Dendritic cells. This matches the scATAC. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} CoveragePlot(object = pbmc, region = "IL1B", expression.assay = "RNA", extend.upstream = 500, extend.downstream = 10000) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Session4_files/figure-html/coveragePlotIL1B-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## QC and Markers At this point I would feel happy with the CD14+ Monocyte annotation. A similar review of other markers for other cell types could help. You can also do this at the cluster level to see if the clusters line up. Always keep in mind the QC. No matter how late you are in the analysis process you could get indicators of a QC issue, which would prompt you to go back and tweak. ## QC and Markers What to look for as a QC issues is similar to scRNAseq: * Non-specific markers * Uncharacterized markers, markers on non-standard chromosomes/sex chromosomes * Stress related markers * Housekeeping related markers * Markers with low log2FC or driven by very few cells ## Finding All Cluster Markers It's easy to expand finding markers to all Cell Types using FindAllMarkers. This will run FindMarkers, for every group within Idents. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all_markers <- FindAllMarkers(object = pbmc, only.pos = TRUE, test.use = "LR", latent.vars = "nCount_peaks") 3.26e- 2 CD16+ Monocytes chr3-16704644-16705… ``` ::: ::: ## Reviewing Cluster Markers As we did for the single cluster marker results, we can visualize our differentials using Coverage Plots. We can also go back to FeaturePlots and VlnPlots to assess how specific these peaks are. ## Pseudobulk Heatmap of Top Markers Per-cell heatmaps of peaks are very sparse, so instead we sum each cell type's counts into a **pseudobulk** profile. Each cell type is normalised by its total counts (CPM), so cell types with more cells or deeper sequencing don't look more accessible across the board. Each peak is then z-scored across cell types. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) # Sum raw peak counts per cell type, then CPM-normalise using all peaks pb <- as.matrix(AggregateExpression(pbmc, assays = "peaks", group.by = "predicted.id")$peaks) pb_cpm <- log1p(sweep(pb, 2, colSums(pb), "/") * 1e+06) # Keep the top marker peaks and z-score each peak across cell types top_peaks <- unique(top5$gene) mat <- pb_cpm[top_peaks, ] mat <- t(scale(t(mat))) heat_df <- data.frame(peak = factor(rep(rownames(mat), ncol(mat)), levels = rev(top_peaks)), cell_type = rep(colnames(mat), each = nrow(mat)), z = as.vector(mat)) ggplot(heat_df, aes(x = cell_type, y = peak, fill = z)) + geom_tile() + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Row z-score") + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Session4_files/figure-html/markerHeatmap-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: # Pseudobulk differential accessibility {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## Pseudobulk differential accessibility ??
